vecchio: The fundamental constraint underlying our results is that GPU speedup is inherently operation-specific and highly dependent on the computational structure of each step. Normalisation and neighbour graph construction represent ideal GPU workloads, achieving speedups of 88-329x and 44-88x respectively, because they involve high arithmetic intensity and are trivially parallelisable across many data elements. In contrast, data loading from disk and Leiden clustering on small graphs show no GPU advantage or even a CPU advantage, but for different reasons. For data loading the culprit is not bandwidth: at sub-gigabyte dataset sizes PCIe Gen5 (128 GB/s) is far from saturated and the transfer itself completes in milliseconds; what dominates the GPU-side cost is the fixed overhead of CUDA context initialisation and RMM pool allocation, and our pipeline additionally routes `h5py`-based reads through CPU RAM rather than via GPU Direct Storage. Leiden clustering on small graphs is limited by low arithmetic intensity: consistent with the roofline model [@Williams2009], cuGraph's constant-time overhead exceeds CPU's short runtime when the graph has few nodes, and the GPU compute units are not saturated. This heterogeneous speedup landscape has important practical implications for practitioners: GPU acceleration is most valuable for large datasets where the compute-heavy operations dominate overall runtime, whereas on small datasets the overhead of GPU operations may outweigh their benefits.
nuovo: The fundamental constraint underlying our results is that GPU speedup is inherently operation-specific and highly dependent on the computational structure of each step. Normalisation (173-329x), an element-wise operation limited by memory bandwidth rather than by arithmetic, had the largest speedup at every size, and neighbour graph construction (44-88x) benefited strongly from the GPU. The CPU neighbour search, however, ran pynndescent with a single numba thread (Scanpy's default `n_jobs = 1`; Methods); on a separate server, 100 threads made it 1.16, 1.91 and 2.48 times faster at 10,000, 50,000 and 100,000 cells, so against a multi-threaded CPU search the neighbour speedup would shrink to about 76x, 32x and 18x, and at 100,000 cells (95% bootstrap interval 8.6-33.1x) it would fall below that of PCA (36.5x). In contrast, data loading was slower on the GPU at every size tested (0.76-0.85x), and Leiden at 10,000 cells was slower on the GPU only at the first resolution (0.36x, mean of five repeats), an effect of the first cuGraph call in the first repeat (1.70 s against a mean of 0.13 s in repeats 2-5); at resolutions 1.0 and 1.5 the GPU was faster (1.36x and 1.60x). For data loading, CUDA context initialisation and RMM pool allocation took place before the timer (Methods), so the timed GPU step comprised reading the h5ad file through CPU RAM and transferring the matrix to the device; its excess over the CPU (+0.10, +0.55 and +1.38 s at 10,000, 50,000 and 100,000 cells) grew with dataset size, which is consistent with reading and conversion costs rather than with a fixed overhead. In practice, the GPU advantage grew with dataset size, but even at the smallest size tested (10,000 cells) the GPU pipeline was 12.0-fold faster end to end, partly because CPU differential expression took 54.9% of the CPU time; we did not observe a size at which GPU overhead outweighed its benefit. Dicks et al. note that below about 50,000 cells kernel-launch and host-device transfer overheads can make CPU execution comparable or faster [@Dicks2026]; their benchmark workflow excluded differential expression.

vecchio: This step-level heterogeneity extends into multi-GPU scaling behaviour. The relatively modest 12% improvement from 2 to 8 GPUs at 1.3M cells reflects a fundamental constraint imposed by pipeline structure: only PCA and neighbour graph construction exploit distributed GPU computation, while the remaining 95% of wall time is spent on inherently sequential CPU preprocessing or single-GPU operations. This imbalance represents a classic manifestation of Amdahl's law [@Amdahl1967], where the non-parallelised fraction dominates overall speedup. Future frameworks could address this bottleneck by distributing preprocessing operations (e.g., chunked QC and normalisation across GPUs) and parallelising Leiden clustering across partitions, but such changes would require substantial modifications to the existing Scanpy architecture. A practical consequence for resource allocation follows from this constraint: because the marginal speedup of adding GPUs to a single run is only approximately 12%, a DGX H100 node is more efficiently utilised as eight independent single-GPU workers running concurrent analyses (yielding near-linear throughput scaling in the number of concurrent studies) than as an eight-way worker for one analysis at a time. This is a non-obvious but important takeaway for groups operating shared GPU infrastructure: the capital-intensive DGX platform delivers its greatest return when treated as a cluster of eight H100 workstations, not as one 8xH100 supercomputer.
nuovo: In our multi-GPU configuration the expression matrix stayed on one device, so PCA and neighbour search ran on a single GPU whatever the number of GPUs allocated, and the additional GPUs did not take part in the computation; the 12% shorter runtime with 8 GPUs at 1.3M cells came from CPU-side data loading in jobs that ran concurrently, the 8-GPU jobs on a different node from the 2- and 4-GPU jobs (Results). Multi-GPU scaling was therefore not measured in this study. Multi-GPU workflows built on Dask have been reported with RAPIDS on 8 V100 GPUs for 1.3 million cells [@Nolet2022] and with rapids-singlecell on 8 B300 GPUs for 100 million cells [@Dicks2026].

vecchio: Related to this, most of the practical value of the GPU speedup is accessible without a DGX at all. At dataset sizes below 500,000 cells the full standard pipeline fits on a single H100 GPU, and the memory-optimised variant described here extends single-GPU feasibility to 1.3M cells and beyond. Single H100 GPUs are readily rentable on commercial cloud platforms at approximately USD 2 to 4 per hour, so the 120x speedup at 1.3M cells reported here (reducing a 14.5-hour CPU analysis to 7.3 minutes) translates to well under one dollar of compute rental for an entire atlas-scale analysis. Access to a full DGX is therefore not a prerequisite for adopting these methods; the results are directly relevant to individual researchers and small groups with pay-as-you-go cloud budgets.

vecchio: The biological outputs of GPU and CPU pipelines show high agreement despite computing on fundamentally different architectures and hardware. The perfect concordance on HVG selection (Jaccard = 1.000) and PCA loadings (Spearman rho = 1.000) reflects the deterministic nature of these operations given identical numerical inputs. The adjusted Rand indices for Leiden clustering range from 0.908 to 0.963 across different resolutions, entirely consistent with the algorithm's inherent stochasticity across implementations (igraph vs cuGraph) and with published benchmarks of clustering variability in scRNA-seq workflows [@Duo2020]. Floating-point non-associativity in GPU parallel reductions contributes negligibly to observed differences, as the dominant source of variation is the Leiden algorithm's non-deterministic vertex ordering. This level of concordance is reassuring for practitioners: it indicates that GPU-accelerated and CPU-based analyses remain interchangeable for biological interpretation and conclusions.
nuovo: At 10,000 cells, the only size at which we measured concordance, the biological outputs of the GPU and CPU pipelines agreed closely. The perfect concordance on HVG selection (Jaccard = 1.000) and PCA loadings (Spearman rho = 1.000) reflects the deterministic nature of these operations given identical numerical inputs. The adjusted Rand indices for Leiden clustering ranged from 0.908 to 0.963 across resolutions, in a concordance run separate from the timed repeats. Since each pipeline returned identical labels in all five timed repeats at this size, these differences reflect the two implementations and their settings (igraph with two iterations, cuGraph with up to 100) rather than run-to-run stochasticity. From 50,000 cells upwards, however, GPU Leiden labels differed between repeats with a fixed seed in at least one GPU configuration at each size, while CPU labels did not, and other studies report CPU-GPU adjusted Rand indices of about 0.5 for clustering of up to 1.3 million cells [@Nolet2022; @Gardner2025]; whether the two pipelines are interchangeable at atlas scale therefore remains to be shown.

vecchio: Perhaps most importantly, our findings reveal that CPU-side memory pressure during preprocessing, not GPU VRAM, is the binding constraint on scalability at extreme scale. This challenges the common intuition that GPU memory availability limits GPU-accelerated analysis. At the maximum testable scale of 11.9 million cells, aggregate GPU VRAM remained flat at 49 GB (7.6% of the 640 GB total) while stable peak CPU RAM reached 535 GB. Critically, the 12M-cell failure did not occur because CPU RAM was exhausted on average (535 GB is only 30% of the 1.8 TB job allocation): it occurred because transient memory spikes during individual preprocessing operations briefly multiplied the working set past the SLURM cgroup limit (Table 6), most plausibly during Scanpy's own preprocessing operations and the duplication of `adata.raw` that its DE backend requires, although our step-level sampling cannot establish which. The bottleneck is therefore not "RAM being full" in the usual sense but a set of short-lived peaks that the scanpy preprocessing stack is structured to create. Substantial further gains in capacity could be realised through preprocessing frameworks that avoid these transient peaks (e.g., reference-only `adata.raw`, streaming Leiden on partitions, chunked sparse-to-dense transforms), since GPU VRAM remains heavily underutilised even at near-maximum cell counts. The capacity limit is more accurately described as a function of cells x HVGs rather than cell count alone, because the dense scaled matrix materialised during preprocessing must occupy one contiguous CPU allocation of n x HVGs x 4 bytes; with 2,000 HVGs this suggests 20M cells at 1,000 HVGs and 4M cells at 5,000 HVGs as linear-extrapolation operating points. Our ScaleSC-inspired chunked variant indeed reduced aggregate VRAM by a factor of five (49 GB to 10 GB) without improving the cell limit, which further underlines that GPU memory is not the binding resource in current single-cell workflows.
nuovo: In the memory-optimised pipeline we tested, GPU VRAM did not limit the number of cells; ScaleSC [@Hu2025] and Dicks et al. [@Dicks2026] reach larger datasets with chunked or out-of-core preprocessing, so the limit we observed belongs to the pipeline rather than to GPU analysis in general. At 11.9 million cells, the largest size completed with this pipeline, aggregate GPU VRAM remained flat at 48.8 GiB (7.6% of the 640 GiB total) while the recorded peak CPU RAM reached 535 GiB, 30% of the 1,800 GiB job allocation. The single run at 12.0M cells stopped with a timeout while the Dask cluster was shut down after neighbour search, so it does not show where the memory limit lies; the runs at 13.7M cells were killed by the system (signal 9) without an out-of-memory message, and our between-step sampling of the parent process cannot show whether transient allocations exceeded the SLURM cgroup limit (Table 6). Preprocessing that avoids dense or duplicated host-side intermediates, as in chunked approaches such as ScaleSC [@Hu2025], is the natural route to larger datasets. Our ScaleSC-inspired chunked variant indeed reduced aggregate VRAM by a factor of five (48.8 GiB to 9.6 GiB) and completed 12.0M cells (it was killed at 15.0M), while host RAM reached 862 GiB, which confirms that GPU memory was not the binding resource in this pipeline.

vecchio: Pseudo-bulk differential expression represents the optimal balance between computational efficiency and statistical rigour. Our DE benchmark confirms that pseudo-bulk aggregation is not merely a statistical best practice (it avoids pseudoreplication and properly accounts for inter-donor variability [@Squair2021]) but also a computational optimisation, reducing runtime by 44x relative to cell-level t-test. GPU acceleration of cell-level DE provides moderate speedups (3-7x) but is ultimately limited by the I/O cost of converting sparse matrices to dense gene chunks. Within cell-level tests on GPU the Wilcoxon rank-sum test actually outperformed the t-test (826 vs 1,656 s), a counterintuitive result that reflects the fact that CuPy's `argsort` maps efficiently onto sparse data whereas the t-test requires dense mean and variance tensors. Beyond these practical considerations, the use of pseudo-bulk becomes essential when interpreting results at scale: at 3.4 million cells, p-values from cell-level tests become uninformative because virtually every gene reaches statistical significance due to the enormous sample size. Effect sizes (log-fold-changes) become the primary quantity of interest, and pseudo-bulk methods coupled with proper count-based models (DESeq2, edgeR) are the gold standard for multi-donor experiments [@Squair2021]. For contemporary single-cell studies, pseudo-bulk should therefore be the default approach on both statistical and computational grounds.
nuovo: In our timing comparison, pseudo-bulk aggregation was the fastest route to a differential expression result (Table 7). Pseudo-bulk aggregation is recommended because it accounts for variation between biological replicates [@Squair2021], and in our benchmark it was also 44 times faster than the cell-level CPU t-test. Cell-level GPU tests finished 3-7 times sooner than the CPU t-test (Table 7); because the CPU Wilcoxon was not run at this scale, these ratios compare time to result rather than measure a within-method acceleration. On the GPU, our Wilcoxon rank-sum implementation, which computes rank statistics without tie correction or p-values (Methods), finished in 826 s and the t-test in 1,655 s; we did not profile the cause. For multi-donor designs, pseudo-bulk aggregation of raw counts analysed with count-based models such as DESeq2 [@Love2014] or edgeR [@Robinson2010] is recommended [@Squair2021]; our pseudo-bulk timing aggregated log-normalised values and used a Wilcoxon test, so it measures computational cost only.

vecchio: Our study contains several limitations that should be considered when generalising these findings. The scRNA-seq benchmark used a single biological dataset (mouse brain E18); performance profiles may differ substantially for datasets with different sparsity patterns, gene counts, or biological characteristics. Concordance analysis was performed at 10,000 cells; larger datasets may exhibit different adjusted Rand index distributions or reveal additional numerical differences. The stress test employing the memory-optimised pipeline is mathematically equivalent to but not implementation-identical to the standard rapids-singlecell workflow, introducing potential differences in how the optimization generalises to other analyses. Spatial benchmarks were conducted on a local RTX 4090 workstation rather than the DGX H100 cluster, precluding measurements of multi-GPU spatial scaling and benchmarking of the full Visium HD 2 um resolution (6.3 million bins). This was not a design choice: the cluster's driver (535.183.01) caps the CUDA runtime at 12.2, and while the scRNA-seq pipeline ran there through forward compatibility, the GPU components of the spatial stack did not, and the container could not be downgraded to a driver-compatible RAPIDS release without breaking the spatial dependencies (Methods). A conservative driver policy on shared production hardware is reasonable, since driver upgrades routinely break unrelated Python environments for every other user of the node, but it is itself a practical constraint on deploying GPU spatial pipelines, and one that the current software stack makes harder to work around than it should be. Scaling analysis was confined to a single DGX H100 node (1-8 GPUs); we did not benchmark multi-node configurations (e.g., 16 GPUs across two nodes interconnected by InfiniBand) because the near-flat wall time observed from 2 to 8 GPUs already indicates that the dominant bottleneck lies in CPU-side preprocessing and single-GPU graph operations (Leiden, UMAP), neither of which would benefit from additional nodes and both of which would be further penalised by inter-node communication latency. A further limitation concerns the multi-GPU configuration itself. Because the standard single-GPU pipeline exceeded 80 GB VRAM at 500k and 1.3M cells, those dataset sizes could only be run through the Dask-CUDA hybrid, in which the preprocessing steps had no distributed GPU route and therefore executed on the host CPU. The 75% CPU-preprocessing fraction we report is thus a property of the software stack available at the time of benchmarking rather than an intrinsic limit of GPU acceleration, and it should be expected to shrink as distributed preprocessing implementations mature. A second limitation concerns the memory instrumentation of the stress test itself: CPU memory was sampled between pipeline steps and for the parent process only, so the reported peaks are lower bounds and the attribution in Table 6 is indicative rather than measured. Resolving it would require continuous sampling of the whole process tree, or the peak usage recorded by the scheduler's cgroup, neither of which we collected. Finally, we did not benchmark integration methods (Harmony, scVI) or multi-sample spatial experimental designs, which represent important directions for ongoing work.
nuovo: Our study contains several limitations that should be considered when generalising these findings. All scRNA-seq experiments used mouse brain cells from CELLxGENE Census: a random sample for the scaling benchmark and the full 3,436,470-cell selection for the stress test, replicated by concatenation beyond that size, and a 3.4M-cell subset of it (202 donors) for differential expression; performance profiles may differ for other tissues and for datasets with different sparsity patterns or gene counts. Concordance analysis was performed at 10,000 cells; larger datasets may exhibit different adjusted Rand index distributions or reveal additional numerical differences. The CPU baseline was a SLURM allocation of 100 logical CPUs on a node with 224, and we did not measure how Scanpy runtimes scale with the number of threads. In the hybrid runs at 1.3M cells, Scanpy QC took 188.2 s with 32 allocated CPUs and 186.6 s with 100, which suggests that some steps are largely single-threaded; the speedups are therefore relative to this allocation, not per core. The stress test employing the memory-optimised pipeline is mathematically equivalent to but not implementation-identical to the standard rapids-singlecell workflow, introducing potential differences in how the optimization generalises to other analyses. The GPU part of the spatial benchmark ran on an RTX 4090 workstation, while its CPU reference ran on a DGX node; multi-GPU spatial analysis and the full Visium HD 2 um resolution (6.3 million bins) were not benchmarked. This was not a design choice: the cluster nodes we used ran drivers 535.247.01 (1-, 2- and 4-GPU runs) and 535.183.01 (8-GPU runs and stress test), which cap the CUDA runtime at 12.2, and while the scRNA-seq pipeline ran there through forward compatibility, the GPU components of the spatial stack did not; a container rebuilt on RAPIDS 24.06 with CUDA 12.2 passed basic GPU tests on a node with driver 535.183.01 but failed the spatial smoke test at the initialisation of CUDA libraries, and was not pursued (Methods). Driver versions on shared production hardware thus constrain which GPU software stack can be deployed. Scaling analysis was confined to a single DGX H100 node (1-8 GPUs); we did not benchmark multi-node configurations (e.g., 16 GPUs across two nodes interconnected by InfiniBand), and since our multi-GPU configuration did not distribute any step (Results), it gives no indication of how a distributed pipeline would behave across nodes. A further limitation concerns the multi-GPU configuration itself: at 500k and 1.3M cells we ran only the Dask-CUDA hybrid, in which, as implemented, preprocessing ran in Scanpy on the host CPU; rapids-singlecell 0.14.1 provides Dask-based routes for QC, normalisation, log1p, scaling and PCA that we did not use. The share of the timed total spent in CPU preprocessing (data loading, QC, normalisation and HVG selection) in the 8-GPU hybrid runs at 1.3M cells (78.0%, mean of five repeats) is thus a property of our configuration, which ran preprocessing in Scanpy on the CPU, rather than an intrinsic limit of GPU acceleration. A second limitation concerns the memory instrumentation of the stress test itself: CPU memory was sampled between pipeline steps and for the parent process only, so the reported peaks are lower bounds and the attribution in Table 6 is indicative rather than measured. Resolving it would require continuous sampling of the whole process tree, or the peak usage recorded by the scheduler's cgroup, neither of which we collected. Finally, we did not benchmark integration methods (Harmony [@Korsunsky2019], scVI [@Lopez2018]) or multi-sample spatial experimental designs, which represent important directions for ongoing work.
